items.title: FCA Handbook, SYSC 15A: Operational resilience
items.quote: in the event of a severe but plausible disruption to its operations
items.why: The binding rule for firms in scope: identify important business services, set an impact tolerance for each, map the people, processes and technology behind them, test against severe but plausible scenarios and run a lessons learned exercise. Applies to the firms listed in SYSC 15A.1, not to businesses generally.

items.title: Operational resilience
items.locator: Opening section and 'Operational resilience requirements for firms'; last updated 15 September 2026
items.quote: Firms in scope of our operational resilience rules had until 31 March 2025
items.why: Source of the deadline in the brief. Defines operational resilience as the ability to prevent, adapt and respond to, and recover and learn from operational disruption, and explains impact tolerances as the maximum tolerable disruption.

items.title: CrowdStrike outage: lessons for operational resilience
items.locator: Sections 'Our general observations following the outage' and 'Observations on ensuring the resilience of infrastructure'
items.quote: Firms reflected on the need to identify single points of failure within their infrastructure and technology stack
items.why: The UK regulator's review of the 19 July 2024 outage. Firms that had mapped their important services and tested severe scenarios recovered faster. It reports that third-party issues were the leading cause of operational incidents reported between 2022 and 2023. Financial sector only; no AI system was involved.

items.title: Critical third parties: strengthening UK financial services
items.locator: Sections 'What the regime means' and 'Designated Critical Third Parties'
items.quote: Firms remain responsible for managing their own third-party risks in line with our existing operational resilience and outsourcing requirements.
items.why: Concentration risk in law. Designation regulations came into force on 13 July 2026 for four providers (Amazon Web Services EMEA SARL, Google Cloud EMEA Limited, Microsoft Ireland Operations Limited, Oracle Corporation UK Limited). Oversight covers their systemic services to the financial sector only and does not move responsibility away from the firm.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 32: Security of processing
items.quote: the ability to restore the availability and access to personal data in a timely manner in the event of a physical or technical incident
items.why: The one general legal duty that touches recovery: where personal data is processed, security measures include, as appropriate, resilience of systems, timely restoration and regular testing. It protects access to the data, not continuity of the service as such.

items.title: Cyber Assessment Framework, Principle B5: Resilient networks and systems
items.locator: Principle B5 description and guidance on resilience preparation; version 4.0, reviewed 6 August 2025
items.quote: consideration is also given to how operation of the essential function can continue in the event of technology failure or compromise
items.why: Source of the quotation. Names manual processes as contingency, asks for business continuity and disaster recovery plans that are tested, and for an understanding of the order of actions needed to restore service. Written for operators of essential functions.

items.title: Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.quote: System Operators shall develop and tailor their disaster recovery plans to account for specific attacks aimed at AI systems.
items.why: The AI-specific recovery expectation. Provision 5.3.1 adds that operators should ensure that a known good state can be restored. Voluntary code; framed around attacks, not supplier outage or withdrawal of a model.

items.title: Cyber security breaches survey 2025/2026
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology and Home Office
items.quote: A similar proportion of businesses (33%), and a smaller proportion of charities (20%) had a business continuity plan that covered cyber security.
items.why: Source of the figure. Among small businesses the share fell from 53% to 44% in a year. The question is about continuity plans that cover cyber security; it does not ask about AI dependencies or whether the plan was tested.

items.title: Guidelines for secure AI system development
items.publisher: National Cyber Security Centre, with the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and partner agencies
items.locator: Section 2 'Secure development', 'Secure your supply chain' (PDF page 12); section 3 'Secure deployment', 'Develop incident management procedures' (PDF page 14)
items.quote: You are ready to failover to alternate solutions for mission-critical systems, if security criteria are not met.
items.why: International comparator: guidance issued jointly by the UK centre and agencies of other countries. Asks providers to have an alternative ready for mission-critical systems. Addressed mainly to providers of AI systems, so a deployer reads it as a question to ask suppliers.

items.title: Independent Review of NATS (En Route) Plc's Flight Planning System Failure on 28 August 2023: Final report (CAP 2993)
items.quote: Reverting to manual mode reduces this capacity to approximately 60.
items.why: Official review of an automated system failing with both primary and backup down. The manual fallback existed and kept flying safe, but handled about 60 flight plans an hour against 700 to 900, and over 700,000 passengers were affected. Shows that a fallback must be sized, not just present. The cover is dated 31 May 2024; the regulator's page gives first publication as 14 November 2024. Not an AI system.

items.title: SS1/21 Operational resilience: Impact tolerances for important business services
items.quote: The PRA expects firms to be able to remain within impact tolerances for important business services, irrespective of whether or not they use third parties
items.why: The prudential regulator's expectations alongside the FCA rule already listed: the recovery target applies whether the service is run in-house or by a supplier, including a supplier within the same group. March 2022 version, updating March 2021. Banks, building societies, designated investment firms and insurers only.

items.title: Financial Stability in Focus: Artificial intelligence in the financial system
items.publisher: Bank of England, Financial Policy Committee
items.locator: Executive summary and the section on operational risks in relation to AI service providers
items.quote: Growing concentration in the supply of AI-related services could increase risks to the financial system.
items.why: The UK authority's statement of AI concentration risk: firms rely on vendor-provided models, cloud computing and data aggregators, and the committee expects third-party exposure to keep increasing as models grow more complex. A financial stability view of the financial sector; it sets no requirement on firms.

items.title: The Financial Stability Implications of Artificial Intelligence
items.locator: Executive summary, first bullet; section 4.2.1 and Table 4
items.quote: The market for these products and services is also highly concentrated
items.why: International comparator on concentration: reliance on specialised hardware, cloud services and pre-trained models has increased third-party dependencies in AI. A report about the financial sector by an international body; it places no requirements on firms.

items.title: Principles for Operational Resilience
items.locator: Principle 3 (business continuity planning and testing); also Principles 5 and 6
items.quote: Banks should have business continuity plans in place and conduct business continuity exercises
items.why: The international standard behind the UK rules: continuity plans exercised against severe but plausible scenarios, dependencies on third parties managed, and response and recovery plans kept. Written for banks; it stands in here for ISO 22301, whose own pages refused automated reading.

items.title: Learning lessons from the cyber-attack: British Library cyber incident review
items.locator: Section Six, 'Learning lessons from the attack', lesson 6 (page 17 of 18); Section Three on recovery
items.quote: Business continuity plans for the total outage of all systems need to be practised regularly
items.why: A public body's own account of recovering from a total systems outage. Its lesson is that plans for a total outage must be practised as well as plans for individual systems, and it found that reliance on legacy systems was the main reason recovery took so long. A self-review by the organisation affected; a ransomware attack, not an AI failure.

items.title: An Empirical Characterization of Outages and Incidents in Public Services for Large Language Models
items.quote: Understanding their outages, and particularly measuring their failure-recovery processes, is becoming a stringent problem.
items.why: Research on the question itself: measures outages and recovery times across eight public large language model services from three providers and finds differences in how long failures take to resolve and how well they are isolated. The abstract records acceptance at the ACM/SPEC performance engineering conference (ICPE 2025); only the abstract page was read. Based on providers' own status reports.

items.title: Picking on the Same Person: Does Algorithmic Monoculture lead to Outcome Homogenization?
items.publisher: arXiv (Bommasani, Creel, Kumar, Jurafsky and Liang)
items.quote: the same systems, or systems that share components (e.g. training data), are deployed by multiple decision-makers
items.why: Research on concentration from the point of view of the people affected: when many organisations share one model or data source, the same individuals can be failed by all of them. Published at NeurIPS 2022; tested on fairness benchmarks, with mixed results for shared foundation models. About outcomes, not outages.

items.title: CAA Paper 2004/10: Flight Crew Reliance on Automation
items.locator: Executive Summary, pages v to vi
items.quote: has left pilots less proficient in manual skills but still required, on occasions, to take control in time critical situations
items.why: Evidence on the manual fallback wearing away: a research review for the UK aviation regulator, written at Cranfield University, on crews becoming dependent on automation. It says little structured research existed and relies partly on interviews. From 2004 and from aviation; an analogy for AI, not a study of it.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.locator: Table 4 (MANAGE function), MANAGE 2.3; also Table 1, GOVERN 6.2
items.quote: Procedures are followed to respond to and recover from a previously unknown risk when it is identified.
items.why: The AI-specific standard for recovery. GOVERN 6.2 adds contingency processes for failures in third-party data or AI systems. Voluntary; a United States framework.
